sections.body: The AI Researcher is about how artificial intelligence is used in research and teaching across ten areas. It covers literature review, citation mapping, quantitative and qualitative analysis, grants, writing and peer review, course design, research data, laboratory work, and integrity rules. In practice, AI tools help search and summarize papers, extract claims, suggest citations, run statistical checks, draft text, generate code, and simulate experiments. They also support teaching by helping design courses, generate practice problems, and give feedback. The work is not fully automated discovery, it is mostly assistance, triage, and pattern finding under human review. This site's library holds 288 research papers and 13608 extracted claims, which shows the kind of material these tools operate on.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts are mature, such as citation mapping, literature search, and reproducible quantitative pipelines, where AI can retrieve, link, and check results at scale. Other parts remain fragile, including qualitative coding, peer review, and grant writing, because context, novelty, and judgment are hard to formalize. Large language models can produce fluent summaries and plausible citations, but they can also invent references, miss nuance, and reproduce bias from training data. Reproducibility is still limited by closed models, changing versions, and unclear evaluation. Governance and integrity rules are developing, but enforcement and disclosure norms vary across fields and institutions. The honest limit is that AI can accelerate many research tasks, yet it cannot be trusted as an autonomous author, reviewer, or arbiter of truth.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader starts with Literature Review and Evidence Synthesis to see how AI finds and summarizes prior work, then moves to Citation Mapping and Discovery to trace how ideas connect across papers. Quantitative Analysis and Reproducible Work covers statistics, code, and repeatable pipelines, while Qualitative Analysis and Mixed Methods deals with text, interviews, and coding where meaning matters more than counting. Grant Proposals and Funding and Academic Writing and Peer Review show where AI helps draft, critique, and manage submissions, though both areas carry strong integrity risks. Course Design and Teaching turns the same tools toward classrooms, and Research Data and Repositories addresses storage, metadata, and sharing. Laboratory Automation and Simulation covers robotic experiments and computational models, and Governance, Ethics and Research Integrity sits above all of them as the rules that constrain the rest.
